title: Coming home
hookLine: he returns to Kapilavatthu; young Rahula asks for his inheritance and is given the teaching

cards: Going home after years away is its own kind of nervous. The streets look smaller. Everyone knows the old you.
Remember the night Siddhartha left Kapilavatthu: the palace, his wife Yasodhara asleep, their newborn son Rahula beside her. He didn't wake them.

Now, years later, the story goes, word reaches his father, King Suddhodana, that his son has become a well-known teacher. The king sends messengers begging him to visit, and he comes. But not the way a prince comes home.
He walks into his hometown with a crowd of monks, and in the morning does what monks do: house to house with a bowl, asking for food.

teach.b: Later tradition fills in the scene. The king is mortified. My son, begging, in my own city?
Our family has never done this. The Buddha answers that his family now is the line of Buddhas before him, and this is their custom. Then comes the moment the old monastic texts do record.
Rahula is a small boy now. His mother, Yasodhara, sends him to his father with a message: go and ask him for your inheritance.
So the boy stands close to the teacher everyone's talking about, and the texts say he told him, pleasant is your shadow, monk.
When the Buddha gets up and walks away, Rahula follows: give me my inheritance, monk.

teach.h: THE BOY IS GIVEN THE TEACHING.
teach.b: Give me my inheritance. The Buddha doesn't hand over land, or gold, or a crown. He turns to Sariputta, the wise friend from yesterday, and asks him to ordain the boy.
Rahula becomes a novice, a young monk in training. The reasoning, as the commentaries tell it: the wealth he's asking for brings trouble and ends; I'll give him an inheritance that doesn't.
The texts are honest that this hurt. King Suddhodana, who had already lost two sons to the homeless life, now loses his grandson too. He goes to the Buddha and says: when you left home, it was pain.
When Nanda left, the same. And now Rahula. Please, don't let children be ordained without their parents' permission.

teach.h: A GRANDFATHER'S GRIEF, A NEW RULE.
teach.b: The Buddha agrees, and makes it a rule: no child is to be ordained without a parent's consent.
One family's grief, written into the monastic code for every family after.

how: In some Theravada countries boys spend a time as novices, with Rahula as their model, and the monastic code asks for parents' permission before a child is ordained, a rule traced to King Suddhodana's request.

o: his return to Kapilavatthu as a monk with a bowl
Siddhartha's return to the palace to be king
the monks' return to the Deer Park for the rains

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.
p: the son who asked for his inheritance
the king who asked for a new rule

s: the Buddha gave Rahula a share of the kingdom
he had Sariputta ordain him: the teaching as inheritance.
a child needs a parent's permission to be ordained
the rule came from King Suddhodana's grief.
Sariputta ordained Rahula at the Buddha's request
the teaching, not land or gold, was his inheritance.

games.q: you're the Buddha. your young son follows you, asking over and over for his inheritance. what do you give him?
o: a share of the palace and land.
a kind word, and send him home.
the teaching: he's ordained as a novice.
games.why: he asks Sariputta to ordain the boy. and when the grandfather grieves, he makes a rule that parents must consent.

practice: Bring to mind something you inherited that wasn't money: a way of laughing, how someone fixed things, a saying, a recipe, a habit of patience. Trace it back: who gave it to you, and who gave it to them?
Stay with that line of hands, as far back as it goes.

wordCard.voice: Coming home. The Buddha returns to Kapilavatthu with a bowl, and his son Rahula, asking for an inheritance, is given the teaching.

orig.note: Pali: inheritance, heritage. What Rahula asked for.

carryVoice: Your line: the real inheritance. Not land or gold, but the teaching. Day sixty-nine, and nearly seventy.

sources.ref: Jataka Nidanakatha; Dhammapada commentary (return to Kapilavatthu)
